Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it was 5:55 a.m.
  • Industry observers note that following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget.
  • Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

Industry observers note that following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government intends to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

Recent findings suggest that but here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

Industry observers note that if the fresh debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

This development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social concerns, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that for 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

It has been revealed that russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary.".

The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are prepares for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, people born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on latest debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that but the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

It has been revealed that the key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

Industry observers note that at the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, this also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an vital point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year.".

It has been revealed that A £116m transfer fee would automatically place anyone under the spotlight. Of late, it has appeared that Elliot Anderson has assumed a prominence anyway, and not always in ways he would have wished. A first return to Nottingham Forest was notable for the challenge he lost to Xavier Schlager that led to Liam Delap galloping clear to score. A meeting with Spain’s World Cup winners was curtailed by a red card for fouling Lamine Yamal; naively, really, given it brought the dual punishments of a dismissal and a penalty.

Industry observers note that so if it is safe to say Manchester City needed Anderson’s equaliser against Fulham, it feels equally true that he did. “Nice moment for him, nice moment for us,” noted Enzo Maresca. City were facing up to the prospect of a fourth straight league defeat. Anderson’s first top-flight goal since an extraordinarily expensive move averted that.

Sources indicate that it offered an illustration of his considerable qualities – and, his mishap at the City Ground notwithstanding, Anderson has been one of City’s finest players in their decidedly mixed season – as well as an idea of how best to deploy them. “We used him today for the first time since the season started as an attacking midfielder,” Maresca explained.

In a recent development, A problem for much of this season is that Anderson has seemed to be playing centre midfield on his own which, even for a player who commanded a nine-figure fee, posed certain difficulties when he was outnumbered. It had felt all the more needless when City’s midfield rebuild came at a record cost.

Industry observers note that with Enzo Fernandez reduced to a cameo, his wanderlust taking him to the bench, and Ayyoub Bouaddi starting, Anderson had a partner. “Ayyoub and Elliot were both really good,” said Maresca. It was not a one-stop solution to bring City solidity: they still conceded, for the 18th occasion in their last nine games, and looked too open. “We need to find a way to keep clean sheets,” Maresca admitted.

In a recent development, but Bouaddi’s presence helped liberate Anderson and there were two moments to demonstrate what he can do when unleashed in the final third. The first was his leveller, a crisp, clean volley from the edge of the box, almost as impressive technically as his strike at the Etihad Stadium for Forest last season. “Fantastic goal,” said Maresca.

It came after Fulham had cleared a corner so arguably Anderson would have been in the same position if Fernandez was not on the pitch. Not when he almost got a winner, though: eight yards out, angling a shot just wide after linking up with Erling Haaland, following the kind of box-crashing run that players like Ilkay Gundogan and Kevin De Bruyne have made when used as No 8s by City. They have instead tended to be Fernandez’s remit this season.

It has been revealed that and if Fernandez is the conundrum, rather than Anderson, there is nevertheless the case that a double act really brings the best out of him. Until his early exit, he excelled alongside Declan Rice in a duo in Madrid. “It has been an interesting week,” said Anderson, which rather underplayed it.

A problem for Maresca is that, even when identifying a way of using Anderson, City still floundered. This was another incoherent display as the longest winning streak between two clubs in English football came to an end. “We knew we lost the last 20 times we played Manchester City but I told [the players] we would have the chance to beat them if we play with courage, with character,” said Alvaro Arbeloa.

Industry observers note that fulham’s first point against City since 2011 was a sign of the progress under the Spaniard, following draws against Liverpool and Manchester United. Arbeloa knocked City out of the Champions League last season when with Real Madrid. He highlighted his prowess with lesser players as Fulham pressed man-for-man, played a variant of 4-2-2-2 and deservedly led.

Industry observers note that the instigator was Oscar Bobb, sold by City in January, with a driving run on the right. Rodrigo Muniz’s first touch took him past Abdukodir Khusanov. His second was placed in the top corner. The striker celebrated by putting the ball up his shirt to mark his wife’s pregnancy. Muniz admitted he struggled last season when she had a miscarriage. It is too trite to say he looked a player reborn, but he gave Fulham a threat.

The opposing No 9 thought he had levelled. A disputed decision ensured otherwise, referee Thomas Bramall ruling Haaland had kicked the ball out of Bernd Leno’s hands when he bundled it over the line. “I had the ball in my hands,” the goalkeeper said. “I had the feeling I controlled the ball and Haaland crashed into me and slid into me.” City disagreed. “From my point of view it is quite clear that it is not a foul,” said Maresca. He said Haaland concurred, but the City top scorer may wish he had met Iliman Ndiaye’s cross with a better finish at the first time of asking.

It has been revealed that it was not the only example of wastefulness. Haaland blazed over when released by Foden. Only three of City’s 15 shots were on target. They could have lost it. After recent errors, there was a redemptive element to Gianluigi Donnarumma’s saves from Bobb and Muniz. City’s winless streak nevertheless continued. “We don’t like this kind of moments in terms of four games in a row,” said Maresca. For Anderson, though, a different game brought a different status, as scorer and saviour.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics.

According to recent reports, thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

Against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It has been revealed that it was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

Industry observers note that as in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

In a recent development, as much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he remarked, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”.

The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

The score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a significant game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Sources indicate that spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a fresh version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Recent findings suggest that tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel stated. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”.

In a recent development, ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, mentioned England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

Industry observers note that “We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”.

Industry observers note that tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

“It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he mentioned. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

In a recent development, “The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was vital to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

Sources indicate that “We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”.

Melania Trump is a special adviser for her son’s dating life.

The First Lady recalled the cautionary advice she gave her and President Donald Trump’s 20-year-old son Barron Trump when it came to his romantic life.

It has been revealed that “I always say it’s a dangerous world out there,” Melania said in the Nov. 20 episode of her latest Prime Video docuseries MELANIA, “and be careful.”.

And beyond his dating life, the 56-year-old noted she’ll be there for Barron “anytime he wants to have my advice or input.”.

According to recent reports, “We have very open communication regarding life. I will always be there for him,” she continued. “I am, and I will always be. And he knows that he’s my priority, and he will always be my priority.”.

Plus, as Melania quipped, “I'm a very cool mom to Barron, and I remind him all the time.".

But while the former model has prioritized motherhood, she has been vocal about not strutting the path of parenthood alone. That’s why she was grateful to have her late mom Amalija Knavs, who died in 2024, to help raise Barron.

“My mother was the epitome of love and warmth, and for Barron, a grandmother who filled every moment with joy and wisdom,” Melania told USA Today in May. “Every story she read to Barron sparked his imagination, and every game they played strengthened their bond.”.

Now, the Melania author is passing down the hard-earned advice she gained from raising Barron.

Sources indicate that “To all the young mothers out there: Shower your children with love and support and always communicate openly,” she continued. “See them as their own unique individuals, not merely as extensions of yourself.”.

And when it comes to ensuring a bright future for the next generation, Melania added, “Guide them with wisdom but establish a foundation of freedom where they can carve their own life path.”.

For a closer look at the branches of Melania’s family tree, keep reading….

Ivana Trump was the first wife of President-elect Donald Trump. Born in Gottwaldov, Czechoslovakia—now Zlín of the Czech Republic—in 1949, she rose to fame as a competitive skier. And, thanks to her marriage to Austrian ski instructor Alfred Winklmayr in 1971, Ivana was able to travel often outside of Czechoslovakia.According to her book Raising Trump, the model met Donald three years after her 1973 divorce during a New York trip, where she'd traveled for a Canadian fashion show ahead of the Montreal Olympics. They wed in 1977 and welcomed three kids: Donald Trump Jr. born in 1977, Ivanka Trump born in 1981 and Eric Trump born in 1984.The pair's divorce was finalized in 1992 following his affair with Marla Maples, whom he later married. However, Ivana—who then married Riccardo Mazzucchelli for two years followed by Rossano Rubicondi for less than a year—and Donald remained on good terms.“Donald during the divorce was brutal,” she told ABC News in 2017. “He took the divorce as a business deal, and he cannot lose. He has to win. So he took about two years. And after the final situation was straightened up, we would just talk and we are friends.”Ivana died in 2022 at age 73. According to NBC News, the New York City Medical Examiner remarked she died of “blunt impact injuries” and that her manner of death was an accident. A senior NYC official with direct knowledge added the circumstances were consistent with a fall on the stairs in her New York apartment.

In 1977, Ivana and Donald welcomed their eldest son Donald Trump Jr. He graduated with a Bachelor’s degree in finance and real estate from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School in 2000 and began working for his father’s organization The Trump Organization in 2001, where he now serves as the executive vice president. Don Jr. is also a director for both Trump Media & Technology Group Corp and PublicSquare Holdings and part of 1789 Capital firm. In addition, he's been involved in his dad’s political campaigns, including speaking at rallies and the Republican National Convention during his father's presidential runs.Don Jr. shares five children with his ex-wife, model Vanessa Haydon: Kai (who also made a speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention) Donald III, Tristan, Spencer and Chloe.Don Jr. was previously engaged to Fox News alum Kimberly Guilfoyle. However, he recently confirmed their split."Kimberly and I will never stop caring for each other," he told Page Six Dec. 13, "and will always keep a special bond."Don Jr. has since been linked to socialite Bettina Anderson. As for Vanessa, she is dating Tiger Woods.

Four years after the arrival of Don Jr., Donald and Ivana became parents to daughter Ivanka Trump. Before her father’s presidency, the University of Pennsylvania alum worked at The Trump Organization. But after he was elected in 2016, the fashion brand founder—who had her own eponymous line—took on the role of Advisor to the President.After her dad unveiled he would be running for president again in 2024, Ivanka revealed she would be stepping out of the political arena to focus on her family with husband, former White House senior advisor Jared Kushner, and their children Arabella, Joseph and Theodore. “I love my father very much,” she said in part of a 2022 statement obtained by NBC News. “This time around, I am choosing to prioritize my young children and the private life we are creating as a family. I do not proposal to be involved in politics.”.

Born in 1984, Eric Trump is the third child of Ivana and Donald. He graduated with a degree in finance and management from Georgetown University.Like his brother, Eric works as executive vice president of The Trump Organization, which he joined in 2007. He is also president of Trump Winery.Eric is married to Republican National Committee co-chair Lara Trump, with whom he shares kids Luke and Carolina.

Marla Maples is Donald’s second wife, whom he met while still married to Ivana.

It has been revealed that in Raising Trump, Ivana wrote the actress approached her about the affair during a trip to Aspen in 1989. Still, Marla stated on a 2018 episode of the ABC podcast Journeys of Faith with Paula Faris that she “never considered” herself a mistress. "My intention was to never bring hurt," she continued. "Do I wish more than anything that we could have had this relationship after his divorce papers were signed? Absolutely. I mean, with all my heart. How much heartache would it have saved so many people if I had seen that piece of paper before we got involved? But it didn't happen that way." Marla and Donald welcomed daughter Tiffany Trump in 1993, and the couple wed later that year. However, the Dancing With the Stars alum and the 47th commander in chief unveiled their separation four years later and finalized their divorce in 1999.

After her parents’ breakup, Tiffany Trump relocated with her mother to California. "She moved us out of Upcoming York to get out of the spotlight and let me grow up and find my own identity versus being in the shadow of a name or growing up very young with all that pressure,” Tiffany told People in 2016. “So, she wanted me to have a chance to have a normal childhood. As normal as possible. I think that she did well in that.” She released her 2011 single “Like a Bird" and graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 2016 with a B.A. in sociology, focusing on law and society. She then went to Georgetown Law School, where she graduated with a JD in 2020. In 2022, Tiffany wed Michael Boulos. Her father announced they're expecting their first baby during an October 2024 speech at the Detroit Economic Club. "She’s an exceptional young woman," he said during his remarks. "And she’s going to have a baby. So that’s nice.”The little one made his debut on May 15, 2025."Welcome to the world our sweet baby boy, Alexander Trump Boulos," Tiffany wrote on X on his birthday. "We love you beyond words! Thank you for coming into our lives!".

Melania Trump is Donald’s third wife and current First Lady of the United States. Born in Mesto, Slovenia in 1970, she is the second First Lady to be born outside of the U.S. and the only First Lady to become a naturalized U.S. citizen.Melania met Donald in Fresh York in 1996 while she was working as a model. “It was a massive fashion party that my friend organized, fashion week, and he invited me,” she recalled on a 2016 episode of On the Record With Greta Van Susteren. “That’s how we met with Donald.” Melania and Donald married in 2005, and they welcomed son Barron Trump the following year. In 2024, she released her memoir Melania and she's set to appear in a documentary. Melania has also spoken about where she will spend her time during her husband's second presidency.

"I will be in the White House," she told Fox & Friends in an interview that aired Jan. 13. "When I need to be in Fresh York, I will be in New York. When I need to be in Palm Beach, I will be in Palm Beach. My first priority is to be a mom, to be a first lady, to be a wife. And once we're in on January 20, you serve the country.".

Born in 2006, Barron Trump is Donald and Melania’s only child. While he has lived a more private life—relocating with his parents from Newly introduced York to live in Washington, D.C. and then Florida—it looked like he might enter the political world after he was selected in May 2024 as a Florida delegate to the Republican National Convention. However, Barron declined the offer."While Barron is honored to have been chosen as a delegate by the Florida Republican Party,” a statement from Melania’s office shared with NBC News at the time noted, “he regretfully declines to participate due to prior commitments.”Like studying, perhaps, with Barron starting his freshman year at New York University in 2024. "He was accepted to a lot of colleges," his father told the Daily Mail in an interview published Sept. 4. "He's a very smart guy, and he'll be going to Stern, the business school, which is a great school at NYU."However, Melania told Fox & Friends in her interview that Barron will come and visit his family at the White House, and he was there for his father's inauguration ceremony in January 2025.

Life as a Wag in the transfer window

📅 08 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour.
  • Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away.
  • Sources indicate that and the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital.".

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

Sources indicate that and the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age.".

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Industry observers note that jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she indicates. "We just met and we clicked.".

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Industry observers note that blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to promptly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," claims Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she notes.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control.".

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it.".

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season.

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Industry observers note that last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is right now a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a fresh team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere.".

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier.

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines.

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship.

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham.

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle.

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she notes.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

Recent findings suggest that "At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved.".

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us.".

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

Recent findings suggest that "But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved.".

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica notes.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football.".

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," notes Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

Recent findings suggest that "Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative.".

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," notes Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't blueprint to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she claims.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place.".

She claims they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," notes Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

Industry observers note that "The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the upcoming strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing.".

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs.

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you.".

Being sensible financially is also notable.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she indicates. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control.".

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

In a recent development, "We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

"In football, you don't get bored!".

Thomas Frank’s Crystal Palace bow ends in own-goal heartbreak

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Thomas Frank suffered defeat in his first game as Crystal Palace boss as Dwight McNeil’s late own goal condemned them to a 3-2 loss at Coventry.
  • Frank, who was sacked by Tottenham in February, oversaw his first game for a third London club but was unable to stop them from losing for a fifth successive match in the Premier League.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Frank suffered defeat in his first game as Crystal Palace boss as Dwight McNeil’s late own goal condemned them to a 3-2 loss at Coventry.

Frank, who was sacked by Tottenham in February, oversaw his first game for a third London club but was unable to stop them from losing for a fifth successive match in the Premier League.

Frank’s tenure got off to the worst start possible when Taiwo Awoniyi put the hosts in front with his second goal of the campaign, but Palace instantly responded through Yeremy Pino.

An all-action first half continued as Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s sublime strike put Coventry back in front before Jorgen Strand Larsen’s first goal since September pulled Palace level again.

It looked like Palace would come away with a point until McNeil inadvertently bundled the ball into his own net to secure Coventry back-to-back home wins.

Frank Lampard’s side are growing in confidence in front of their own supporters and picked up a third win at the Coventry Building Society Arena.

Lampard was wary of the visitors starting strongly with a new boss, but it was his side who drew first blood when Jack Rudoni played the ball across for Awoniyi to stab a first-time effort into the far corner.

The hosts were left wondering how they were not two to the good when, seconds after Carl Rushworth’s save down one end, the Sky Blues broke through Awoniyi and he rounded Dean Henderson but saw his effort blocked heroically by Axel Disasi on the goal-line.

They were made to pay shortly afterwards as Palace levelled.

Daichi Kamada sent a cross in towards Strand Larsen who saw his failed scorpion attempt bounce kindly for Pino and he lashed home from close range.

Coventry regained their advantage on the half-hour mark courtesy of a sublime hit by Sakamoto.

Rudoni had assisted the first and was the creator again as he whipped a cross to Sakamoto who took a lovely touch with his chest before lashing a shot past Henderson from outside the box.

Palace came from behind for a second time on the stroke of half-time. Pino turned creator with a cross onto the head of Strand Larsen, who had sprung the offside the trap and nodded the ball beyond Rushworth.

Henderson was called into action to stop Coventry from going ahead for a third time as he dived to his right to palm Rudoni’s effort behind.

Palace were in the ascendancy and looking most likely to get their noses in front.

Strand Larsen was first onto a low cross by Pino but he was stopped by Rushworth and Bobby Thomas made a crucial block to stop substitute Evann Guessand from sweeping the ball home.

It proved vital as Coventry snatched a winner. Brandon Thomas-Asante’s initial header was saved by Henderson but the ball bounced off McNeil and rolled over the line.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Golloria can’t conceal her thoughts on Huda Beauty’s apology.
  • After the makeup brand’s founder Huda Kattan apologized to the beauty influencer for how her tech giant handled discontinuing their darkest setting powder Coffee Cake and replacing it with Coco Truffle, Golloria shared her thoughts on the response.
  • “I appreciate your apology and you taking the time to get back to me,” Golloria posted in the comments of Kattan’s Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Golloria can’t conceal her thoughts on Huda Beauty’s apology.

After the makeup brand’s founder Huda Kattan apologized to the beauty influencer for how her tech giant handled discontinuing their darkest setting powder Coffee Cake and replacing it with Coco Truffle, Golloria shared her thoughts on the response.

“I appreciate your apology and you taking the time to get back to me,” Golloria posted in the comments of Kattan’s Nov. 20 Instagram post. “Speaking from both my experience as a shade consultant and as a dark skinned woman whose shade options are directly affected by this decision, I don’t think Coco Truffle should replace Coffee Cake. And that’s just the honest truth.”.

The TikToker explained that she heard Huda Beauty’s reasoning that Coffee Cake wasn’t doing well with consumers, but added that she didn’t think the two shades were “interchangeable,” noting that “a shade occupying a similar depth in a range doesn’t necessarily mean it serves the same complexions.”.

Sources indicate that “You’ve said several times that you want to better serve dark skinned women, and part of that is listening to the women telling you that Coffee Cake already works for them,” the 25-year-old continued. “That feedback should help guide what you preserve as you expand the range.”.

She also added that darker skinned women “deserve variety in both depth and undertone,” and that having both shades would help create that inclusion. Instead, Golloria shared in her own Instagram caption that she felt Huda Beauty was “doing what's easiest for the brand instead of what's needed by the women you say you want to serve.”.

“Inclusion means making room for our differences,” she wrote, “not asking us to settle for whatever is most convenient for you to offer.”.

As for Kattan, while the beauty founder did not reply to Golloria’s comment, she explained in her apology video that she was sorry for how the conversation about the shade replacement had been handled with Golloria, especially as it was happening during a busy time for the brand and when Kattan herself had to undergo emergency surgery for a ruptured breast implant in April.

According to the 43-year-old, her team found that Coffee Cake was “not something that a lot of people have shared positive feedback with us on,” adding that they “definitely thought we could make it a lot better.”.

According to recent reports, the decision led them to launching Coco Truffle as a replacement for Coffee Cake, first as a pressed powder, then as a loose powder—although it was not yet widely available.. But after hearing from their consumers, Kattan realized they should have done a better job being more inclusive with their shades.

“Inclusivity is not about, ‘Yes, done, check, we're inclusive.’ That to me is some of the things that are wrong with the industry,” she noted. “It's 2026. We can do better. We can do better and I think brands should be doing better in 2026.”.

And while they will be reworking Coco Truffle to make sure it’s available “as quickly as possible,” she also regretted fully removing Coffee Cake from their lineup.

“We should have kept it in stores,” Kattan stated, “because at the end of the day, if some people liked it, we should have kept it in stores until there was something better available.”.

She also once again apologized for not having better communicated all of this to Golloria initially, although she was hopeful that the beauty influencer and Huda Beauty fans would appreciate Coco Truffle.

“I'm hoping to give you guys a shade that you guys really, really love, and all the beautiful rich skin tone girls and boys feel really represents them,” Kattan shared, “and is perfect for their skin tone.”.

How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

Industry observers note that "I've always been a bit cautious about this glitch in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he unveiled a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently.".

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

Industry observers note that this week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also mentioned AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

It has been revealed that nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market.".

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this latest openness from unexpected quarters. "It indicates that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," mentioned Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

Industry observers note that "But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play.".

According to recent reports, the idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they mentioned AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, but Herrmann stated it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

"On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens.".

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

In a recent development, dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he remarked, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

Recent findings suggest that however, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living.".

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," stated Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible.".

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?".

Industry observers note that this, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," mentioned Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Luca Williams-Barnett lived up to the hype with a sparking display on his full debut for Tottenham to inspire a 2-0 win over Ipswich.

Roberto De Zerbi turned to the 18-year-old after two bright cameos and the highly-rated Spurs attacker delivered with aplomb, scoring on his first Premier League start after 15 minutes before a mazy run set up Dominic Solanke at the start of the second half.

After Williams-Barnett made his senior debut at the age of 16 last season, the clamour for the teenager to play has only increased during a difficult last 12 months and with injuries to Mathys Tel and Mykhailo Mudryk, the England Under-19 international grasped his chance to show why he has been hailed as a “special talent” by De Zerbi.

It was not a completely positive afternoon for De Zerbi with Savio forced off late on with a problem on his comeback after a seven-week lay-off.

However, this victory made it three home wins in a row for Tottenham in the Premier League for the first time in two years in further evidence a corner may have been turned in N17.

The excitement was palpable when it was confirmed Williams-Barnett would earn a first start for Tottenham with De Zerbi making six changes from the defeat at Leeds.

Gary O’Neil also shuffled his pack and went to a back five, but Ipswich started strongly and Antonin Kinsky was forced to deny Abdoul Ouattara and Zian Flemming in quick succession.

With De Zerbi in the stand due to a touchline ban, Spurs slowly started to get on top with Solanke curling wide before Williams-Barnett had the crowd on their feet with two dangerous crosses after lightning-quick step-overs.

Solanke went close again with a header across goal before Christian Walton denied the Tottenham forward from another set-piece, but the breakthrough arrived in 15th minute and via teenage sensation Williams-Barnett.

Pedro Porro was the architect with a wonderful cross from the right-hand side and Williams-Barnett demonstrated excellent hunger to get ahead of Ouattara before he bundled in with his left knee.

It made Williams-Barnett the youngest Tottenham scorer in the Premier League since Gareth Bale in 2007.

Spurs almost made it 2-0 by the half hour mark but Mohammed Kudus curled a fine free-kick against a post.

Ipswich threatened again soon after; the busy Conor Gallagher blocking an effort by Exequiel Palacios before Kinsky claimed a corner and James Maddison received a booking for a pull back on Julio Enciso.

There was still time for Williams-Barnett to have a header saved and Walton thwarted a Maddison curler before the break.

With the game still in the balance, Spurs required a second goal and Williams-Barnett stepped up to make the difference again in the 52nd minute.

After Williams-Barnett picked up the ball inside his own half, the 18-year-old raced past Darnell Furlong and sent across an inch-perfect cross for Solanke to slide home his third goal this season.

Williams-Barnett accepted the acclaim before he left to a standing ovation with 26 minutes left.

After Walton prevented an own-goal by Ipswich captain Dara O’Shea, a minute’s applause in memory of Danny Kelly followed in the 69th minute and whilst Savio was forced off not long after his cross hit a post, Tottenham made it four wins in five.

Tech Report: 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.
  • As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane notes.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Industry observers note that watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

How dropping deep helps Kane score.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box.

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles.".

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

According to recent reports, kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength.

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

Recent findings suggest that through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space.

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal.

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

Sources indicate that "I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play.".

In a recent development, in the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch.

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with.".

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

Industry observers note that "When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball.".

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

Industry observers note that "The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre.".

Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

Recent findings suggest that "I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off.".

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track].".

The Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

Sources indicate that with Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net.

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back.".

Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders.

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch.

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner.

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead.

Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Sources indicate that frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It mentioned he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

It has been revealed that by the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he mentioned.

With Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is said to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Nonetheless, Frank is noted to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

There is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

For now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

According to recent reports, his Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

According to recent reports, the futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

Harry Kane is England’s upcoming leading appearance-maker after passing Peter Shilton’s record last week – and he hasn’t been the only player tipped to reach the milestone over the years.

Shilton’s record of 125 Three Lions caps had stood since he made his final appearance for his country at the 1990 World Cup, before Kane played his 126th cap against Croatia, then made it 127 against Spain on Sunday.

Wayne Rooney had previously finished agonisingly short on 120, with David Beckham winning 115 caps, Steven Gerrard reaching 114, Ashley Cole making it to 107 and Frank Lampard clocking up 106.

Another player who looked on course to surpass Shilton at one point was Michael Owen, who won his 89th cap at the age of just 28, but didn’t add to his tally as injuries derailed his career.

Asked whether he feels he would have made it to 126 if the injuries hadn’t hit, the former striker is philosophical about it.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m not that bothered about that, I had my time,” he told FFT. “In little moments when you think back over your career, you think of things, but that’s across the board, isn’t it?

“If I didn’t get injured then, would I have won more Golden Boots? Would I have won the Ballon d’Or more? Would I have won more of anything? You just never know. It’s one of those things.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“There’s no question about it, if I had Harry Kane’s constitution, there’s no doubt I would have scored many, many, many more goals than I did, played many, many, many more games than I did, and all the rest of it.

Industry observers note that “But I’m happy with my lot, I played 89 times for England – that’s quite a lot. That’s just life, isn’t it? You can’t spend your life thinking ‘What if?’”.

Owen reserved praise for Kane, who has scored an incredible 93 goals during his 127 caps.

Industry observers note that “What he’s done is extraordinary really,” Owen stated, speaking in association with soccer betting odds. “He’s fine-tuned his game to become one of the most lethal players on the planet. It’s strange because he’s not the fastest, he’s not got a trick that always beats a defender, it’s pure efficiency.

“His finishing is just lethal. I think he’s the best finisher on the planet by some way, whether it’s left foot, heading, placing the ball, power, his penalties are brilliant. He’s practised and practised all his life to become so elite.

Recent findings suggest that “You need so many things when you’re a player. A lot of it comes naturally, but you need to hone your skills as well. Harry has been one of the most hard-working players of this generation and deserves everything he gets.”.
